title: Can a sealed class be abstract, and what is the impact on inheritance?
shortTitle: Can a sealed class be abstract, and what is the impact on inheritance?

s1_definition.profdef: Yes. A sealed class may also be `abstract`. The `sealed` and `abstract` modifiers are orthogonal: `sealed` controls which classes may extend it, while `abstract` controls whether it can be instantiated directly. An abstract sealed class cannot be instantiated and may declare abstract methods, and its concrete behaviour must be provided by its permitted subclasses, each of which must be declared `final`, `sealed`, or `non-sealed`. This combination is the idiomatic way to define a closed family of related concrete types sharing a common abstract base.
s1_definition.analogy: Imagine National Bank of India defines an abstract concept of "Account" that describes what every account must do — report its balance, apply monthly processing — but you can never walk in and open a plain "Account"; you must open a specific product. At the same time, head office seals the concept so only three named products may ever be an Account. So "Account" is both a blueprint you cannot instantiate directly (abstract) and a closed family with a fixed membership list (sealed). The two rules work together: a blueprint with a locked guest list.
s1_definition.oneliner: A sealed class can be abstract — `abstract` stops direct instantiation while `sealed` restricts who may extend it, and both constraints apply at once.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** Yes. A sealed class may also be `abstract`. The `sealed` and `abstract` modifiers are orthogonal: `sealed` controls which classes may extend it, while `abstract` controls whether it can be instantiated directly. An abstract sealed class cannot be instantiated and may declare abstract methods, and its concrete behaviour must be provided by its permitted subclasses, each of which must be declared `final`, `sealed`, or `non-sealed`. This combination is the idiomatic way to define a closed family of related concrete types sharing a common abstract base.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** Imagine National Bank of India defines an abstract concept of "Account" that describes what every account must do — report its balance, apply monthly processing — but you can never walk in and open a plain "Account"; you must open a specific product. At the same time, head office seals the concept so only three named products may ever be an Account. So "Account" is both a blueprint you cannot instantiate directly (abstract) and a closed family with a fixed membership list (sealed). The two rules work together: a blueprint with a locked guest list.

**One line to remember:** A sealed class can be abstract — `abstract` stops direct instantiation while `sealed` restricts who may extend it, and both constraints apply at once.

sections.s2_technical:
`sealed` and `abstract` answer two different questions. `abstract` answers "can I create an instance of this class directly?" — the answer is no, and it allows the class to have abstract methods that subclasses must implement. `sealed` answers "which classes are allowed to extend this class?" — the answer is only the listed permitted subclasses. Because they govern different things, Java lets you combine them freely: `public abstract sealed class Account permits SavingsAccount, CurrentAccount, LoanAccount { ... }`.

An **abstract sealed class** is extremely common and idiomatic. You use it when there is shared state and behaviour across a closed set of concrete types. The abstract base holds the common fields and concrete helper methods, declares abstract methods for the parts that vary, and the sealing guarantees that only your known subclasses exist. Each permitted subclass still must be `final`, `sealed`, or `non-sealed`, exactly as for any sealed type.

The **impact on inheritance** is twofold. First, because the base is abstract, no code can do `new Account(...)`; callers must create one of the concrete permitted subclasses. This pushes all instantiation to the leaves, which is usually what you want for a type family. Second, because the base is sealed, the set of subclasses is fixed and known to the compiler, so the abstract methods have a finite, known set of implementations. This enables exhaustive handling: a `switch` over the abstract sealed type can cover every subclass without a `default`, and the compiler verifies completeness.

A subtle point is the interaction with **abstract methods and exhaustiveness**. You can implement varying behaviour either by overriding an abstract method in each subclass (classic polymorphism) or by pattern-switching on the sealed type in a service. Both are valid. Overriding keeps behaviour with the data; switching centralises behaviour in one place and benefits from compiler-checked exhaustiveness. In banking you often use both: core invariants as abstract methods on the base, and cross-cutting policies as exhaustive switches in services.

A senior nuance is that an abstract sealed class can still have **constructors**, which the subclasses call via `super`, letting you enforce invariants on common fields even though the base cannot be instantiated alone. Another nuance is that if you make the base `sealed` but **not** abstract, it can be instantiated and extended by its permitted subclasses, which is occasionally useful but less common than the abstract form. A final nuance is that an abstract sealed class combined with final record or final class leaves is the cleanest Java encoding of an algebraic data type, giving you a non-instantiable, closed, polymorphic family that the compiler fully understands — ideal for modelling a bank's fixed set of account products or transaction states with strong guarantees.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — National Bank of India wants a common `Account` base that holds shared fields like id, holder, and balance, and defines shared behaviour like crediting money, while forbidding anyone from creating a plain, typeless account. The base must be abstract so only real products can be opened. This is the abstract part.

Problem 2 — The bank also wants to guarantee that only savings, current, and loan products can ever be accounts, so no rogue subtype appears. The base must be sealed with a permits list. This is the sealed part, and together they form an abstract sealed class.

Problem 3 — Interest calculation varies by product, so the base declares an abstract `monthlyInterest` method that each concrete subclass implements, and a service also runs an exhaustive switch to apply a regulatory cap, demonstrating both overriding and exhaustive switching over the sealed family.

In the mini-project we define `abstract sealed class Account permits SavingsAccount, CurrentAccount, LoanAccount`, with shared fields, a constructor, a concrete `credit` method, and an abstract `monthlyInterest`. The three final subclasses implement it, and a service applies an exhaustive switch, logging each computation.

The code contains: the abstract sealed base, three final subclasses, an `InterestService`, and a demo.

sections.s5_journey:
Input data: a savings account for Rajesh with 1,000,000, a current account for Priya with 250,000, and a loan account for Rajesh with 3,000,000.

Step 1 — `main` cannot write `new Account(...)` because the base is abstract. Instead it creates concrete products. Each subclass constructor calls the abstract base's constructor via `super`, which sets the shared id, holder, and balance fields, enforcing those invariants even though the base itself is never instantiated alone.

Step 2 — For each account the service calls `cappedMonthlyInterest`. Inside, a `switch` pattern-matches the three permitted subclasses. Because the base is sealed, the compiler knows the complete set and verifies the switch is exhaustive, so no `default` is needed.

Step 3 — Each case calls the subclass's overridden `monthlyInterest`. Savings computes 3% per year divided by 12 on 1,000,000, giving 2,500.00. Current returns zero. Loan computes 9% per year divided by 12 on 3,000,000, giving 22,500.00, all using `BigDecimal` with half-up rounding.

Step 4 — The service then applies the regulatory cap of 20,000.00 centrally with `min`. Savings 2,500.00 and current 0 are below the cap and pass through. Loan's 22,500.00 exceeds the cap and is reduced to 20,000.00. This shows the abstract-method override and the exhaustive switch working together.

Step 5 — Each capped interest is logged with the product type and id.

```
2026-10-26 14:10:15 [INFO] SavingsAccount SAV2001 monthly interest = Rs.2500.00
2026-10-26 14:10:15 [INFO] CurrentAccount CUR3001 monthly interest = Rs.0.00
2026-10-26 14:10:15 [INFO] LoanAccount LN5001 monthly interest = Rs.20000.00
```
sections.s5b_flow:
```
  abstract sealed class Account permits {Savings, Current, Loan}
     │ cannot `new Account(...)`  (abstract)
     │ subclasses call super(id, holder, balance)
     ▼
  create SavingsAccount, CurrentAccount, LoanAccount
     │
     ▼
  cappedMonthlyInterest(a) → switch (exhaustive, sealed → no default):
     Savings → monthlyInterest() = 1,000,000 × 3%/12 = 2500.00
     Current → monthlyInterest() = 0.00
     Loan    → monthlyInterest() = 3,000,000 × 9%/12 = 22500.00
     │
     ▼ apply CAP 20000.00 via min()
     Savings 2500.00  (< cap)   → 2500.00
     Current 0.00     (< cap)   → 0.00
     Loan    22500.00 (> cap)   → 20000.00
```

sections.s6_takeaway:
Yes, a sealed class can also be abstract, because sealed and abstract control two different things. Abstract controls whether the class can be instantiated directly, and the answer is no, plus it allows abstract methods that subclasses must implement. Sealed controls which classes are allowed to extend it, limiting them to the permitted list. Since they govern different concerns, Java lets me combine them, and the abstract sealed class is actually the most idiomatic form.

I use an abstract sealed class whenever there is shared state and behaviour across a closed set of concrete types. The abstract base holds the common fields and concrete helper methods, declares abstract methods for the parts that vary, and the sealing guarantees only my known subclasses exist. Each permitted subclass still has to be final, sealed, or non-sealed. A nice detail is that the abstract base can still have constructors that the subclasses call through super, so I can enforce invariants on the shared fields even though the base itself can never be instantiated.

The impact on inheritance is twofold. Because the base is abstract, nobody can create a plain base instance, so all instantiation is pushed to the concrete leaves, which is exactly what I want for a type family. Because the base is sealed, the set of subclasses is fixed and known to the compiler, so the abstract methods have a finite, known set of implementations, which enables exhaustive handling.

In my banking project the account base is abstract and sealed, permitting only savings, current, and loan. It holds id, holder, and balance, provides a concrete credit method, and declares an abstract monthly-interest method. Each product overrides the interest calculation, and my interest service also runs an exhaustive switch over the sealed family to apply a regulatory cap centrally, with no default branch because the compiler knows the set is complete. So I get the best of both: shared behaviour and enforced invariants from the abstract base, and a closed, compiler-checked family from the sealing, which is the cleanest way to model a bank's fixed set of products.

---

keyPoints: sealed: restrict which classes can extend/implement
permits: explicit list of allowed subclasses
Subclass must be: final, sealed, or non-sealed
Enables exhaustive switch/pattern matching — compiler checks all cases
